title: Just Like Heaven
summary: A–E–Bm–D, one bar each, at a gallop. Great for open-chord changes, then for learning to voice-lead with triads so the chords flow into each other.
notes: Chord progression and practice parts only. The melody line here is an original guide-tone exercise, not the song's riff or vocal.

bass.name: Driving eighths
bass.steps: R R R R R R R R

keys.name: Left-hand drive, right-hand pad
keys.left: R R R R R R R R

lessons.title: Four open chords at speed
lessons.goal: Change A, E, Bm, D on every downbeat at 100 bpm.
body: Bm is the one that trips people up. Play it as the A-shape barre at the 2nd fret: it's the same move as your B chord in Fire on the Mountain, with one finger changed.
Look for anchors: from E to Bm your hand moves up, from Bm to D your third finger can stay close to the B string.
steps: Play along at 80 bpm with the open chords variation.
Mute rhythm guitar and keep the eighths going on your own.
Step the tempo up by 8 until it gets messy, then back off one notch.

lessons.title: Let the triads flow
lessons.goal: Play the progression on the top three strings, moving as few fingers as possible.
body: These triads all live between the 2nd and 6th frets. A and E share the note E, Bm and D share D and F#. Hold the shared notes and move only what has to move.
This is voice leading, and it's the trick that gets you out of big barre shapes.
steps: Play "Triads, top strings" along with the track.
Watch the fretboard and notice which dots stay put between chords.
Try "Picked triads" to hear each note ring separately.

lessons.title: Move it to the middle strings
lessons.goal: Find the same progression on strings 2, 3 and 4.
body: Same idea, one string set lower. The shapes change because of the B string's tuning, so they're worth learning separately.
steps: Set the fretboard's string set to 2-3-4 and look at the shapes for each chord.
Play the "Triads, middle strings" variation along with the track.
Alternate: one pass up top, one pass in the middle.

lessons.title: Driving strum
lessons.goal: Accent the downbeats while keeping eighths even.
body: Capital D is a full accented downstroke; lowercase u is a light upstroke on just the top strings. That contrast is what makes the strum gallop.
When it's comfortable, try the sixteenth push in the Build section.
steps: Play along at 100 bpm.
Switch to the Build section and try the sixteenth push variation.

lessons.title: A melody made of thirds
lessons.goal: Hear how the third of each chord makes a melody on its own.
body: The guide-tone line starts each bar on the chord's third: C# over A, G# over E, D over Bm, F# over D. Everything else just walks to the next one.
Switch the fretboard labels to intervals and watch for the teal 3.
steps: Listen to the guide-tone line twice.
Mute it and play it from the tab on the Sheet page.
Improvise in A major pentatonic, but start each bar on the third.

lessons.title: Left-hand drive
lessons.goal: Steady eighth-note roots in the left hand under a held right-hand chord.
body: This is the bass player's job given to your left hand: the same note eight times per bar, perfectly even. The right hand holds the chord for the whole bar.
Keep the left hand relaxed and bounce from the wrist. Accent beat one slightly.
steps: Left hand alone at 90 bpm.
Add the right hand, changing on each downbeat.
Mute keys and play along.

lessons.title: Voice leading A–E–Bm–D
lessons.goal: Play the four chords in one hand position with shared notes held.
body: Look at the keyboard on Part: A is A–C#–E, E is G#–B–E, Bm is B–D–F#, D is A–D–F#. E stays put from A to E, and D and F# stay put from Bm to D.
That's the same idea as the guitar triads lesson: move only the notes that have to move.
steps: Play each change slowly and say out loud which notes stay.
Play along with Voice-led chords.
Then try the bell arpeggio on top.

lessons.title: The driving beat
lessons.goal: Understand why this groove feels like it's running.
body: Kick on every beat plus the 'and' of 3, snare on 2 and 4, eighth-note hats. The floor-tom version swaps hats for toms, which makes it darker and more tribal.
Every fourth bar, the fill version stops the hats and rolls the snare into the next phrase.
steps: Solo drums and compare Driving with Floor-tom pulse.
Loop Driving with a fill and count the four-bar phrase.
In Capture, make a fill of your own for bar four.

lessons.title: How FM operators work
lessons.goal: Hear what an operator’s ratio, level and envelope each do, and why the wiring matters.
body: An operator is a sine wave with its own level and its own envelope, nothing more. A carrier is an operator you hear. A modulator is wired into another operator’s pitch and wobbles it so fast that you don’t hear a wobble: you hear a new tone colour.

The ratio picks which overtones appear. They land at the carrier plus and minus steps of the modulator: at 1:2 that’s 1, 3, 5…; at 1:3.5 it’s 1, 2.5, 4.5, 6… Whole-number ratios put them on the note’s own harmonics, so it sounds pitched, like an organ or brass. In-between ratios put them between the harmonics, so it rings like a bell. The level, called the index on a modulator, picks how many of them are loud: more index, brighter.

Each operator’s envelope is what makes the tone move. A modulator that dies away before its carrier lets the brightness fade before the note does: a bell. A short burst on a high-ratio modulator is an electric piano’s tine. A modulator that swells in slower than its carrier is a brass attack.

The algorithm is the wiring. Carriers side by side are layers you mix, two sounds in one. A stack, a modulator modulating a modulator, makes far more overtones from the same knobs. Feedback, an operator modulating itself, pushes a sine towards a sawtooth’s buzz. So a patch looks hand-tuned because it is: each operator is one ingredient (the body, the attack, the shimmer) and the algorithm decides which you hear and which only colour the others.

Build sounds in this order and FM stops being guesswork: one carrier alone, one modulator at 1:1, raise its index, change the ratio, then shape the modulator’s envelope. Add operators only once you know what the first two are doing.
steps: Play a key in the FM lab with Sine chosen: one line on the spectrum, at the note, and a plain wave.
Raise operator 2’s index slowly (turn on Hold notes to keep a note ringing): lines appear either side, evenly spaced, and the wave gets a kink.
Set operator 2’s ratio to 2, then 3, then add a fine of .50: at 3.5 the lines leave the harmonic grid and it turns into a bell.
Give operator 2 a short decay and no sustain: the note gets darker as it rings, while operator 1 keeps going.
Start from E-piano and try Stack and Two pairs with the same operators: same ingredients, different wiring, a different instrument.

With the SMK-37 connected (Keyboard in the top bar), play the lab from its keys and turn K5–K8 on their MIDI CC bank for the four operators’ levels. Send to keyboard loads your sound into the SMK’s own FM engine; press PATCH there to keep it.
Play the verse’s chords on the keyboard with a sound you made, while the band plays with the keys muted.

lessons.title: Design a bell for the arpeggio
lessons.goal: Make an FM bell sound and play the arpeggio part on your synth.
body: Bells come from non-whole-number ratios. Try a modulator at 3.5 times the carrier, a fast attack, and a decay of about a second with no sustain. More modulation makes it glassier.
Mute keys, then play the bell arpeggio on your synth: root, third, fifth, octave and back down.
steps: Load Bell in the FM lab, or set up a two-operator patch with a 1:3.5 ratio on your synth.
Shape the decay so each note rings into the next without smearing.
Mute keys and play along.
